text: Involvement of DNA polymerase III in UV-induced mutagenesis of bacteriophage lambda
Anne Brotcorne-Lannoye1, Geneviève Maenhaut-Michel1, and Miroslav Radman2 1ool v  e, o  B nsu J. ono C..R. Univers ar Tour  , place uss,F7551 Pars Cedex 05, F

Summary. It has been proposed that the mutation fixation processes stimulated by SOS induction result from an induced infidelity of DNA replication (Radman 1974). The aim of this study was to determine if mutator mutations in the $E$ coli DNA polymerase III might affect UV-induced mutagenesis.

Using a phage $\lambda$ mutation assay which can discriminate between targeted and untargeted mutations, we show that the polC74 mutator mutation (Sevastopoulos and Glaser 1977) primarily affects untargeted mutagenesis, which occurs in a recA1 genetic background and is amplified in the $r e c A ^ { + }$ genetic background. The polC74 mutation also increases the UV-induced mutagenesis of the bacterial chromosome. These results suggest that DNA polymerase III is involved in the process of UV-induced mutagenesis in E. coli.
Introduction

Ultraviolet light (UV), ionizing radiation and many chemicals cause mutations in $E$ coli and some of its phages via an inducible error-prone repair pathway which is a part of the SOS response (Defais et al. 1971; Radman 1974; Witkin 1976; Caillet-Fauquet et al. 1977). The SOS response is controlled by the recA and lexA genes (review Walker 1984). SOS induced bacterial mutagenesis and Weigle-reactivation of phage are specifically reduced by the umuC (Kato and Shinoura 1977; Walker and Dobson 1979) and uum (Steinborn 1978) mutations. The precise mechanism of SOS induced mutagenesis is not known, but it has been proposed that SOS induction results in a transient decrease in the fidelity of DNA replication (Radman 1974; Caillet-Fauquet et al. 1984). This would facilitate the bypass replication of DNA lesions and lead to the production of both targeted mutations at the site of initial DNA damage, and untargeted mutations at undamaged DNA sites (Caillet-Fauquet et al. 1977; Witkin and Wermundsen 1978). Sequencing data have supported the notions of these two types of mutation in bacterial DNA (Coulondre and Miller 1977) and in DNA phages (Brandenburger et al. 1981; LeClerc and Istock 1982; Wood and Hutchinson 1984; Wood et al. 1984).

DNA polymerase III, which is the replication enzyme of the E. coli chromosome (Kornberg and Gefter 1971) and phage λ DNA (Skalka 1977) was proposed to be involved in the mutation fixation process during bacterial UV mutagenesis (Bridges et al. 1976). To determine if a DNA polymerase III  associated decrease in the fidelity of the replication machinery may alleviate the requirement for SOS induction in UV mutagenesis, we have studied the effect of a series of polC thermosensitive mutator mutations, isolated by Sevastopoulos and Glaser (1977), on UV induced mutagenesis of bacteriophage λ. The use of $\lambda$ DNA as a probe for cellular mutagenic activity makes it possible to separate mutagenesis on undamaged DNA from mutagenesis on damaged DNA (Ichikawa-Ryo and Kondo 1975; Quillardet and Devoret 1982; Caillet-Fauquet et al. 1984; Maenhaut-Michel and Caillet-Fauquet 1984).

Our results show that the polC74 mutation increases untargeted mutagenesis even in a recA background, but has no significant effect on either survival or on targeted mutagenesis. It also increases UV induced mutagenesis of the bacterial chromosome. These results suggest that DNA polymerase III is involved, at least indirectly, in UV induced mutagenesis in $E _ { \mathrm { { \ell } } }$ coli.

Results
1. Effect of different thermosensitive mutations in the polC gene on UV induced mutagenesis of λ phage

To investigate the role of the replication fidelity in UV induced mutagenesis, we have analysed the effect of different $E .$ coli mutator mutations, isolated by Sevastopoulos and Glaser (1977), mapping in the polC (dnaE) gene (see Methods), on UV induced mutagenesis. A series of $E .$ coli polCts mutator mutants, grown at $3 2 ^ { \circ } C$ were infected with unirradiated or UV-irradiated $\lambda$ phages and the progeny phages were analysed to measure separately any effect of polCts mutations on mutagenesis occuring on undamaged DNA (untargeted mutagenesis) and damaged DNA (both targeted and untargeted mutagenesis). The advantages of the forward mutation system $c ^ { + } {  } c$ in particular the use of the thermosensitive cI857 mutation to measure both targeted and untargeted induced mutagenesis, have been described elsewhere (Caillet-Fauquet et al. 1984; MaenhautMichel and Caillet-Fauquet 1984). All the polCts mutants tested revealed an increase in UV induced untargeted mutagenesis but only some of them increased mutagenesis of irradiated phage (Table 2). We have decided to analyse in detail the effect of the polC74 mutation which was found, in a preliminary test, to affect mutagenesis of both irradiated and unirradiated phages.
2. Effect of the polC74 mutation on the spontaneous mutagenesis in E. coli and phage λ

The thermosensitive polC74 mutant has a mutator phenotype at $3 2 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ and a reduced rate of DNA synthesis at $4 2 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ (Sevastopoulos and Glaser 1977). The spontaneous mutation frequency of both bacteria and phage $\lambda$ was increased in the polC74 mutant grown at $3 2 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { \bf C }$ compared with the parental $p o l C ^ { + }$ strain (Table 3). The differences observed in the extent of the mutator effect of the polC74 mutation in the $\lambda c I 8 5 7 {  } \lambda c$ mutation assay and on the three bacterial mutation sites studied may reflect a mutational specificity of the modified polymerase III. the polC74 mutation caused a similar increase in spontaneous mutation frequencies in $r e c A ^ { - }$ and $r e c A ^ { + }$ backgrounds (Table 3).

Figure 1A shows that the polC74 mutant produces higher untargeted mutagenesis than the isogenic $p o l C ^ { + }$ strain, the induced mutants appearing only as mixed plaques $c / c ^ { + }$ . The possibility that the increased frequency of mixed bursts is due to increase in $\lambda$ replication cycle was discounted for the following reasons. It has been demonstrated that UV irradiation of host bacteria decreases $\lambda$ burst size, particularly at high UV doses (Jacob 1954; Caillet-Fauquet and Defais 1977). The same result was obtained with the polC74 and $p o l C ^ { + }$ strains (not shown). Morever the yield of phages produced in unirradiated and UV irradiated polC74 mutant is lower than that found with the $p o l C ^ { + }$ strain whereas the plating efficiency is identical with the two strains (data not shown).

As expected (Ichikawa-Ryo and Kondo 1975; CailletFauquet et al. 1984), untargeted mutagenesis of $\lambda$ phage is suppressed by the recA1 mutation in the $p o l C ^ { + }$ strain (Fig. 1B). But, surprisingly, the double mutant polC74 recA1 was found to be proficient in untargeted mutagenesis (Fig. 1 B), the extent of mutagenesis being higher than in the polC\* recA+ wild type strain and, at low UV doses $( 5 0 ~ \mathrm { { J / m } } ^ { 2 } )$ , even higher than that observed in the single $p o l C 7 4 ~ r e c A ^ { + }$ mutant. However, at high UV doses $( 1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { J } / $ $\mathfrak { m } ^ { 2 \cdot }$ the frequency of induced mutations is lower in the double mutant polC74 recA1 than in the single polC74 $r e c A ^ { + }$ mutant (Fig. 1). Therefore it appears that the polC74 mutation alleviates, at least partially, the necessity for the recA gene product in untargeted mutagenesis. The higher mutation frequency observed at low UV doses in the polC74 recA1 strain, relative to the $r e c A ^ { + }$ parent, may be due to the absence of the $r e c A ^ { + }$ dependent post-replication repair, such that more of unrepaired mutation-inducing lesions persist in the DNA of the E. coli recA mutant.
4. Effect of the polC74 mutation on survival and mutagenesis of UV-irradiated λ phage

We have tested the effect of the polC74 mutation on survival and mutagenesis of UV-irradiated λcI857 phage grown in an unirradiated or UV-irradiated host. The polC74 mutation has no effect on the survival of irradiated $\lambda$ phage grown in either unirradiated or UV-irradiated $r e c ^ { + }$ or recA hosts (not shown). Similar to unirradiated phage, mutagenesis of irradiated phage is higher in the polC74 mutant than in the $p o l C ^ { + }$ parent (Fig. 2A). This increase is largely caused by a higher incidence of mixed bursts (Fig. 3). In contrast the frequencies of pure bursts are similar in $p o l C ^ { + }$ and polC74 bacteria.

To test for possible activation of the RecA1 mutant protein in the recA1 polC74 double mutant, the amount of the RecA1 protein was measured using the highly sensitive immunoradiometric (IRMA) assay for the RecA protein (Salles and Paoletti 1983). The RecA1 protein was readily detected: there was no amplification in the double mutant (Salles B, Calsou P, Brotcorne-Lannoye A, not shown) suggesting that the recA1 gene is not noticeably leaky for its SOS inducing function.
5. Effect of the polC74 mutation of UV induced mutagenesis of the bacterial chromosome

We have analysed the effect of the polC74 mutation on the UV induced production of rifampicin resistant mutants. Figure 5 shows that a larger increase in mutation frequency is observed in the polC74 mutant than in the $p o l C ^ { + }$ strain, particularly at low UV doses. Therefore it appears that the polC74 mutation also increases the number of UV induced mutations in the bacterial DNA (a complete analysis of UV induced mutagenesis of the bacterial chromosome will be published elsewhere).
Discussion

Our intention was to see whether any decrease in the fidelity of DNA replication might alleviate the requirement for SOS induction in UV mutagenesis. By studying polCts mutator mutants affecting the DNA polymerase III, we were able to examine the role of DNA polymerase III and its fidelity in UV mutagenesis. All of the polCts mutator mutants tested were found to affect mutagenesis of phage $\lambda$ by UV light (Table 2). Moreover, all three mutator mutations tested, including the polC74, increased the UV induced mutagenesis of the bacterial chromosome by an order of magnitude (Fig. 5 and data not shown).

We have analysed in detail the effect of the polC74 mutator mutation on UV induced mutagenesis of phage $\lambda$ in a $r e c A ^ { + }$ and a recA background. In the presence of the $p o l C 7 4$ mutation UV produces higher mutation frequencies in both irradiated and unirradiated phage $\lambda$ than it does in the isogenic $p o l C ^ { + }$ strain (Figs. 1 and 2). This increase is most pronounced in unirradiated phages (Fig. 2) and appears to be due exclusively to increased production of mixed $( c / c ^ { + } )$ bursts (Fig. 3). UV induced $\lambda$ phage mutagenesis was observed also in a polC74 recA double mutant (Fig. 4). The survival of irradiated phages, as well as the production of pure $\lambda$ clear mutant bursts which requires irradiation of the target DNA and the umuC gene product (Wood et al. 1984; Maenhaut-Michel and Caillet-Fauquet 1984), are not affected by the polC74 mutation (Fig. 3). These results, together with the fact that the UV induced mutagenesis of the bacterial chromosome is also increased in the polC74 mutant (Fig. 5), indicate an interaction between the polC74 mutant DNA polymerase III and some cellular effect of UV irradiation. The fact that the polC74 mutation strongly affects the untargeted but not the targeted mutagenesis suggests that the mechanisms of the two mutational events are different. Different genetic requirements have been found for the untargeted and targeted mutagenesis (Ichikawa-Ryo and Kondo 1975; Maenhaut-Michel and CailletFauquet 1984). It has been proposed that the mixed bursts reflect genuine replication errors since their frequency is decreased by the post-replicative mismatch repair system (Caillet-Fauquet and Maenhaut-Michel 1982; Caillet-Fauquet et al. 1984). Therefore, the effect of the polC74 mutation appears to occur at the level of UV stimulated replication errors.

The polC74 mutation partially compensates the defect in UV mutagenesis caused by the recA1 mutation. The absence of detectable amplification of the RecA1 protein in the recA1 polC74 double mutant argues against the RecA1- activation due to a possible leakiness of the recA1 mutation (results not shown). The RecA protein was shown to have two different roles in UV induced mutagenesis: one is to inactivate the LexA repressor and thus to induce the umuCD functions (Walker 1984) and the other (which is required even in the presence of the UmuCD proteins) is involved directly or indirectly in the mutation fixation process (Witkin and Kogoma 1984). It was suggested recently that the umuC function may be required only for elongation of DNA synthesis past non-coding DNA lesions (Defais 1983; Maenhaut-Michel and Caillet-Fauquet 1984; Bridges and Woodgate 1984). Untargeted mutagenesis (MaenhautMichel and Caillet-Fauquet 1984; Defais 1983) as well as the misincorporation step in targeted mutagenesis (Bridges and Woodgate 1984) appear not to require the umuC function and are probably associated with DNA polymerase activity.

The polC74 mutator mutation apparently compensates for only one of the two requirements for the RecA protein in UV mutagenesis, probably the misincorporation step which is umuC-independent. Since phage survival and the production of pure mutant burst are not increased in the polC74 recA mutant, it appears that the mutator effect of the polC74 mutation is not sufficient by itself to allow mutagenic translesion synthesis.

In conclusion, our work suggests that DNA polymerase III, and its fidelity, is involved, directly or indirectly, in UV-induced mutagenesis in $E ,$ coli by affecting predominantly the untargeted mutagenesis.
